## Welcome back

- Weeks 7 gave you a menu: t-test, ANOVA, ...
- The second half of the course replaces the menu with **one idea**:

> Most common statistical tests are special cases of the **linear model**. — Jonas Lindeløv, *Common statistical tests are linear models*

- Learn one framework deeply, and you can answer almost any question in this course

## The one equation

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \varepsilon$$

- In R: `lm(y ~ 1 + x1 + x2)`
- The test you want is almost always **a question about one or more β's**
- Different tests = different choices of what goes on the right-hand side

## One sample and paired t-tests

| Classic test      | Linear model      |
|-------------------|-------------------|
| One-sample t-test | `lm(y ~ 1)`       |
| Paired t-test     | `lm(y2 - y1 ~ 1)` |

- The intercept **is** the mean (or the mean difference)
- The test of the intercept against 0 **is** the t-test

## Two groups and many groups

| Classic test      | Linear model                    |
|-------------------|---------------------------------|
| Two-sample t-test | `lm(y ~ 1 + group)`             |
| One-way ANOVA     | `lm(y ~ 1 + group)` + `anova()` |

- With a categorical predictor, R creates 0/1 **dummy variables**
- Intercept = mean of the reference group; each slope = difference from it
- t-test and ANOVA are the *same model* — two groups vs. three or more

## Continuous predictors

| Classic test         | Linear model                   |
|----------------------|--------------------------------|
| Pearson correlation  | `lm(y ~ 1 + x)` (standardized) |
| Simple regression    | `lm(y ~ 1 + x)`                |
| Spearman correlation | `lm(rank(y) ~ 1 + rank(x))`    |

- Slope = change in y per one-unit change in x
- Correlation is just the slope when both variables are z-scored

## Why bother?

- **Fewer things to learn** — and the assumptions are the same ones every time
- **Easy to extend** — add a covariate, an interaction, a random effect
- **Better communication** — an estimate with an interval, not just a p-value
- Weeks 10–14 build directly on this: every new test is a small extension

## A tool for reading models: `marginaleffects`

- Model coefficients depend on how the model was coded (reference levels, interactions, link functions...)
- `marginaleffects` asks questions in the units of the **data**:

| Question | Function |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| What does the model predict? | `predictions()`, `avg_predictions()` |
| How does the outcome differ between groups / treatments? | `comparisons()`, `avg_comparisons()` |
| What's the slope of the outcome in x? | `slopes()`, `avg_slopes()` |
| Custom tests of combinations | `hypotheses()` |

## The same three questions, every week

1.  **Fit** a model (`lm`, `glm`, `lmer`, ...)
2.  **Check** its assumptions
3.  **Ask** the question with `marginaleffects`

- Same workflow Weeks 9–14, only the model in step 1 changes
- Docs: [marginaleffects.com](https://marginaleffects.com)

## Design still matters

- A linear model can't tell you whether the data *can* answer your question
- Randomized treatment → causal estimate; measured predictor → association
- The model describes; the **design** justifies
